hints.title: Count distinct roots of the product
hints.body: Relate the roots of g to the roots of f′ and the extra factor x.
hints.recap: Differentiate a polynomial term by term with the power rule before analysing its roots.
hints.pitfall: Repeated multiplicity does not create another distinct root.
hints.pause: Write down which roots can coincide and must be counted just once.

recall.reminder: Differentiate a polynomial term by term with the power rule before analysing its roots.

hints.title: Build small witnesses
hints.body: Try a quadratic family, varying its vertical and horizontal position to control its roots and its stationary point.
hints.recap: A possibility claim can be proved by one explicit example meeting all the conditions.
hints.pitfall: An example proving one comparison does not settle the other two.
hints.pause: Investigate each proposed comparison by computing both root counts in your trial examples.

recall.reminder: A possibility claim can be proved by one explicit example meeting all the conditions.

solution:
It is enough to exhibit a polynomial for each claimed possibility. In g(x)=xf′(x), zero is always a root; any nonzero derivative roots supply further roots.

For f(x)=x2+1, there are no real f-roots, whereas g(x)=2x2 has one distinct root. Thus M<N.

For f(x)=x2−2x, f has the two distinct roots 0,2 and g(x)=2x(x−1) has the two distinct roots 0,1. Thus M=N.

For f(x)=x2−1, there are two distinct f-roots while g(x)=2x2 has one. Thus M>N. All three are possible: answer H.
knowledgePattern: Construct polynomials exhibiting all comparisons of function-root and x-derivative-root counts
